claims.text: Every statement that reads or changes a table first takes a table-level lock on it (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and table-level locks are held until the end of the transaction.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 13.3.1 Table-Level Locks (locks held until transaction end)

claims.text: SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (the strongest mode).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 13.3.1 Table-Level Locks, ACCESS SHARE; Table 13.2 Conflicting Lock Modes

claims.text: Plain CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) takes SHARE lock: reads continue, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the table block until the build's transaction ends.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, CREATE INDEX (Building Indexes Concurrently: 'locks out writes (but not reads)'); 13.3.1 SHARE

claims.text: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts with every lock mode including the one SELECT takes.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, ALTER TABLE (Notes: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE unless noted); 13.3.1 ACCESS EXCLUSIVE

claims.text: A lock request that conflicts with a request already waiting queues behind it, even if the current holder alone would allow it: C's SELECT waits behind B's waiting ALTER TABLE although A only read.
claims.source_hint: scripts/backend/migration-locks.sh @ stage-4 lines 56-77 and outputs/stage-4/scripts/backend/migration-locks.txt step 3; PostgreSQL 17 docs, 13.3 Explicit Locking

claims.text: lock_timeout aborts any statement that waits longer than the given time to acquire a lock; 0 (the default) disables it. The error is 'canceling statement due to lock timeout'.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 19.11.1 Statement Behavior: lock_timeout; output step 1 and 3

claims.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY lets reads and writes continue; it does two table scans and waits for existing transactions that could modify or use the index to end, so a long open transaction stalls it and it takes longer than a plain build.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, CREATE INDEX, Building Indexes Concurrently

claims.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot be executed inside a transaction block (between BEGIN and COMMIT); refused there, it builds nothing, so the same index name can be created right after (output step 2: error, then 'created').
If a concurrent build fails while scanning the table, it leaves an INVALID index, ignored for querying but still maintained on updates; the fix is to drop it (or REINDEX) and build again.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, CREATE INDEX, Building Indexes Concurrently (invalid index)

claims.text: EF Core executes a migration's operations in a transaction; Up/Down receive a MigrationBuilder, whose Sql(sql) adds a raw SQL operation; Sql(sql, suppressTransaction: true) runs that SQL outside the transaction.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs, Custom migrations operations / MigrationBuilder.Sql(string, bool suppressTransaction); Applying migrations (transactions)

claims.text: pg_stat_activity is a system view with one row per server process (connection); its wait_event shows 'relation' while waiting for a table lock (wait_event_type Lock) and 'PgSleep' during pg_sleep.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 27.2.3 pg_stat_activity and Wait Events (Table 27.11 Lock, Table 27.13 Timeout PgSleep); migration-locks.sh lines 17-25, 42, 67, 71

claims.text: Script: A sleeps 60 s in its open transaction (never commits); `end` terminates a session, rolling it back; until_state polls wait_event; INSERT lock_timeout 2s, ALTER 5s; 200,000 orders; `session` runs one named psql command; donhang_perf built if missing.
claims.source_hint: scripts/backend/migration-locks.sh @ stage-4 lines 6-27, 36-77; scripts/backend/perf-db.sh @ stage-4; psql = PostgreSQL's command-line client (PostgreSQL 17 docs, psql)

claims.text: If the migrate hook (wave 1) fails, the sync stops before wave 2, the api Deployment rollout, so the api Deployment is not updated and the old api keeps serving.
claims.source_hint: Argo CD docs, Sync Phases and Waves / Resource Hooks (failed hook fails the sync); devops.l3.ordering-a-sync

claims.text: Trade-offs: plain build blocks writes, is faster, stays in the migration transaction; concurrent build keeps writes, is slower, needs suppressTransaction, leaves an invalid index on failure; building during a stop costs a planned outage.

Use a plain CREATE INDEX when the table is small and rarely written; use CONCURRENTLY when the table takes writes all day; give a migration a short lock_timeout when long transactions may hold the table, and run it again later.
